title: The open tent
hook: Abraham's tent, open on all sides, is the model of hospitality

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bal tashchit, and its line, waste nothing. Today, a door that stays open.

Midday, in the plains of Mamre. Genesis says Abraham "sat in the tent door in the heat of the day." Not inside, in the shade. At the door. Then he looks up and sees three strangers standing nearby. He doesn't wait for them to knock or ask: "he ran to meet them from the tent door," and bowed to the ground. Abraham, in the worst heat of the day, running toward people he's never met. You met this scene in year one; today, the tent the rabbis saw behind it.
screen: `THE HEAT OF THE DAY.` → `SITTING AT THE DOOR.` → `HE RAN TO MEET THEM.`

segments.voice: Hachnasat orchim. Bringing in guests. First, the tent. The rabbis noticed that Abraham saw his guests before they reached him, and a collection called Avot de-Rabbi Natan says his tent had openings on every side, so a traveler from any direction would find a way in. No front door, no back door. Second, say little, do much. Abraham offers "a morsel of bread." Then he hurries to Sarah for cakes, runs to the herd for a calf, and sets out butter and milk. The Talmud, in tractate Bava Metzia, reads this as a habit of the righteous: they promise little and give much. Third, a startling ranking. Abraham says, "pass not away," and the rabbis read those words as spoken to God: please wait. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, draws a bold lesson from it: welcoming guests is greater than receiving the presence of God. Abraham left a vision to go set out bread. Fourth, the house today. In the Mishnah's Ethics of the Fathers, the sage Yose ben Yochanan says to let your house be open wide, and to let the poor be members of your household. Not guests on a schedule; part of the family. The tent at Mamre becomes a way to keep any kitchen: see people early, go toward them, say less than you give. The door was the place Abraham chose to sit.
screen: `OPEN ON EVERY SIDE.` · `A MORSEL, THEN A FEAST.` · `GREATER THAN A VISION.` · `LET YOUR HOUSE BE OPEN WIDE.` · then, large: `OPEN TENT.`

segments.voice: Let the people around your life pass through your mind: a new neighbor, a colleague eating alone, a friend who's been quiet, a student far from home, and let one face stay. Ask what an open tent would look like for that person this week: a coffee, a seat at your table, a walk, an invitation before they have to ask. Settle on the morsel you'll offer, and quietly plan to give more than you said.
The open tent. Hachnasat orchim, bringing in guests: Abraham at the door, open on every side, running to meet strangers. Today's word.
Your line: open tent. No front door, no back door, a way in from every side. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hachnasat orchim is practiced by inviting guests, including strangers and travelers, to Shabbat and holiday meals, and some synagogues match visitors with host families.

notes: Avot de-Rabbi Natan 7: Abraham's house/tent with openings on every side (the text says four sides) — paraphrased as 'every side'; also found in Genesis Rabbah 48:9. Confirm.
Shabbat 127a: 'hospitality is greater than receiving the Divine Presence', learned from Genesis 18:3; confirm attribution (Rav Yehudah in Rav's name).
Bava Metzia 87a: the righteous say little and do much, from Abraham; confirm.
Genesis 18:1, 18:2, 18:5 fragments quoted from KJV; confirm. 'three strangers' is from the text (18:2).
Avot 1:5 (Yose ben Yochanan of Jerusalem) paraphrased.
